testo: I think it’s possible to give some written or verbal form to the ideas inherent within a film. I think there’s an underlying thesis within all films but the most brilliant ones could have entire essays written about them. I don’t know how useful it is because you will always lose a great deal of the power of the film by trying to reduce a visual form down to a written one but if I can’t write about it then I either don’t understand what the movie is about or there is no real expression done by the filmmaker. I mean the Batman Begins “controlling idea” that you put forward isn’t wrong as much as it is incomplete. That is a central idea of the film but it lacks all of the context or the complexity within it and gives a reductionist view of the ethical and moral difficulties that the film is centered on so strongly. It’s not that you are wrong, it’s that the mode of interpretation, or rather the brevity of the controlling idea creates a false vision. I find the main thematic underpinnings of the film, and the trilogy in general, to be concerning justice. Batman is a vigilante figure who tries to correct the self destructive and morally chaotic Gotham city outside of the jurisdiction and authority of the democratically elected state. However, the principle antagonist to the film, far more than the destructive organized crime groups like Falcone’s organization, is a radical, fascistic militia group who abandon faith in Gothams ability to organically self correct and decided to organize Gotham’s implosion through hallucinatory chemical weapons. So both parties have the same pursuit, with different means of carrying it out. So in essence boiling it down into the catchphrase “It’s not who you are underneath. It’s what you do that defines you” is true, but that could equally be interpreted as a call to heroism and transcending inaction. But I don’t think that’s the primary concern of the movie, because passivity is not the primary threat to Gotham, it is a threat, but a fanatical devotion to principle is what causes Gothams flirtation with oblivion. So I believe that it is not just possible, but stimulating to analyze films while trying to not over intellectualize the experience and devoid it of its emotional power. I actually think it’s necessary, not to see how smart we are or to come up with a single unchallengeable and un disposable interpretation of a film, but to also defend against propaganda as well. I think the Batman example is a great one because the major cultural fascination and obsession with superheroes and the genres natural sympathies with propaganda and fascist impulses are important to recognize. Superheroes becomes cultural icons and tend to be on the verge of worship, they are usually presented as totally altruistic and completely just, ethical discussion regarding their inherent vigilantism is practically nonexistent, and their antagonists are defeated with relish and encouraged by the audience from their immediate introduction. So examining that dichotomy in a post imperial, modern society is important. But as I said before I don’t want to forget the emotional power of a story, but cinema operates on two separate fields, there is the form of visual storytelling and there is the narrative. The form can be discussed, but in much more general terms, it’s a common saying that a picture is worth a thousand words, but a movie is 24 pictures per second for 2-3 hours. So converting the visual form into words has diminishing returns. But I see no reason why we cannot discuss and write about film narrative like you would a piece of literature. To distill the narrative on screen to a concise, well reasoned and observant piece of criticism that acknowledges the moral and ethical implications of the events and the characters behavior, recognizes the thematic content and tries to find with the film itself and the context of the time and creator of the piece the intent behind the expression. A film like 2001 can’t be reduced down to a single line of written prose, but you can write pages and pages about the ways in which Kubrick focuses on evolution, tribal conflict, artificial intelligence and the questions of the metaphysical in the age of science.

> Yet I still spend far more of my free time with what I would consider, easy entertainment. Video games, TV, YouTube, Reddit, and other miscellaneous "activities" are what occupy the most of my time. 

IMHO what is 'easy entertainment' depends upon how much thought the medium stimulates, and also how easily decipherable it is.  For example, I just finished the Brothers Karamazov in audiobook form, I found the language easy to follow even if some of the matters were weighty.  I also listened to the Green Mile, and while that book was less than 1/3 the length of the Dostoevsky tome, I found that it also dealt with weighty matters (even if some of it was supernatural).  Stephen King has a reputation for writing 'easy entertainment' yet I don't think that's fair to his entire body of work.

Movies like Armageddon are most definitely 'easy entertainment' (in fact the less thought one puts into it the more enjoyable the movie is), as was Game of Thrones season 8, which was essentially a non-stop popcorn fest of sex and violence with little to no plot cohesion.  Compare that to Game of Thrones season 1-4, which had intricately crafted scheming and character motivation, and it's IMHO a shame that the series ended on such an 'easy' note.

Just to reiterate, my point is simple, it's not the genre that makes it 'easy', but rather whether or not it stimulates a good amount of thought.

edit - to add another example, Greek dramas tend to be considered 'weighty', yet I remember in high school I read Lysistrata.  That work, while a Greek drama, has more in common with modern pornography than it does with anything 'weighty'.

I highly recommend browsing Roger Ebert's website, and his Great Movies list. Find movies there that you've already seen and that you know you love. Read Roger's comments on them, revisit them to experience what he's talking about first hand if you feel you need to. Then start watching other movies from his list that look interesting to you and reading those reviews as well. 

The Great Movies reviews in particular he takes a deeper look at what works, and you can learn a lot just by looking at the movies through the eyes of someone who made their profession at it. Most importantly though, it's clear that Roger *loved* film, and that enthusiasm comes through constantly. It never feels like an impersonal or clinical analysis; it reads like someone who is excited about what's on the screen, and wants you to be just as excited.

To me, terror and horror are not the same.

Terror is typical of short duration.  Horror may be of infinite duration.

Terror is typically localized.  Horror may be cosmic.

Terror is typically psychologically superficial.  Horror is often psychologically deep.

Terror often has an understood basis. Horror often has a basis that cannot be understood--indeed, some horrors don't seem to have a basis, or that basis is unknowable.

The thing causing the terror can often be destroyed, placated, run away from.  The thing causing a horror often cannot be destroyed, cannot be placated or run from.  It subsumes a being or grinds it away.

I could compare a typical Stephen King terror to a typical H.P. Lovecraft or William Hope Hodgson or Clark Ashton Smith horror.

>There was a bursting as of an exploding bladder, a slushy nastiness as of a cloven sunfish, a stench as of a thousand opened graves, and a sound that the chronicler would not put on paper. For an instant the ship was befouled by an acrid and blinding green cloud, and then there was only a venomous seething astern; where—God in heaven!—the scattered plasticity of that nameless sky-spawn was nebulously recombining in its hateful original form, whilst its distance widened every second as the Alert gained impetus from its mounting steam. (from The Call of Cthulhu by Lovecraft)

Notice that most of that description is necessarily indirect because Lovecraft attempts to describe what cannot be described, or if it can be described, is wholly inadequate, even silly in hindsight.  Human words cannot capture a horror; they often fail.  By contrast, it is usually quite easy to describe the cause of a terror.

The character in the Lovecraft story does not write a bladder exploded, but that is the only thing he could compare some unknown aspect of his experience to--not a sound per se.  He does not write it had a specific stench, but that a thousand open graves is the only thing he could imagine he might compare the smell to--and I do not doubt that is hyperbole upon imagination as that character might not know what even one open grave smells like, let alone a thousand.  He does not write the chronicler knew what the sound was, merely that whatever it might have been, the chronicler does not report it.

I.e. there is a void at the center of the description.  The puny statue which a character describes earlier in the story is almost a parody of the real thing.  After all, characters can hold that statute, but no one would want to be in the grip of Cthulhu.

This differs profoundly from e.g. a teenager with special powers (as in Carrie) or a vampire (as in 'Salem's Lot) or any other typical terror.

I think there're a lot of unfounded assumptions, simplistic neurobiology, and simple misandry in your comment, but I do agree with the last part, and would go further and say that this sex in movies is porn. It’s nothing like any sex I’ve ever experienced (I have a 15 year old daughter so I’ve had sex once-ish) and never seems to relate to the rest of the work in any way. 

Even on the level of a simple action film, it would be possible for John Maclean to have sex with Holly Degenero in a way that underpins or expands on characterization and the strengths of the story, or even for Vision and Scarlet Witch to show the fundamental challenges and strengths of their unique relationship through a sex scene. But that’s nothing that Hollywood could even attempt.

Casablanca is partly about unrequited feelings, and the impossibility, perhaps unreality, of True Love. I definitely think a sexual scene could have been used to explore that - perhaps one that was profoundly useless and unsatisfying, and ended abruptly. Of course that wouldn’t match the stylistics of a monochrome  1940s film, but it is, in theory, possible.

That term I used - ‘sexual scene’ - is key I think. Sex scenes are usually pornographic and unreal, as you say. They are what we hope our own sex might be, and not what our sex actually is. Sexual scenes would be ones involving sexual activity but much more, just as a good action scene involves danger but much more. Again, even Die Hard and The Avengers, at their best, do several things at the same time as their fights. Scenes with action, not John Wick’s scenes of action, which are like pornographic sex scenes in their shallowness.
